faq.a: Skin contains several kinds of touch sensor. When skin is pressed or stretched, the sensor's nerve ending is squashed, which opens tiny channels and starts an electrical signal that travels to the brain.
asks: How does a touch become a signal?

faq.q: How does the body feel pain?
faq.a: Pain sensors, called nociceptors, are bare nerve endings that react to damage, extreme heat or cold, or harsh chemicals. They send warning signals to the spinal cord and brain so you can protect yourself.

Fingertips have far more touch sensors packed into each square centimetre than places like your back, and a large area of the brain handles their signals. That lets you feel tiny bumps, like Braille dots.
asks: Why can fingers feel such small things?
Which part of the body is most sensitive?

faq.q: Why do I pull my hand away before I feel the pain?
faq.a: Pain signals reach the spinal cord, which sends a command straight back to your arm muscles. This reflex happens before the message has finished reaching your brain, so you move first and feel the pain a moment later.
asks: Why do I react before I feel it?

faq.a: Deep pressure sensors called Pacinian corpuscles are made of layers like an onion. They respond to quick changes in pressure, so they are great at sensing vibrations, such as a buzzing phone or a humming machine.

facts: Fingertips have one of the highest densities of touch receptors in the body.
Pain-sensing nerve endings are called nociceptors.

quiz.say: You touch a hot pan and pull away before it hurts. What made you move so fast?
quiz.show: What makes you pull away from a hot pan so fast?

options.show: A reflex through the spinal cord
options.say: A reflex through the spinal cord

quiz.why: Pain signals reach the spinal cord, which sends a command back to the muscles before the brain has fully registered the pain.

wrong.1: Seeing the pan is much slower than the reflex.
wrong.2: The pan does not push you; your own muscles move your hand.
